title: Where is the sound?
hookLine: a king takes a lute apart looking for its sound (SN 35.246)

cards: A king or his minister has never heard a lute. One evening the sound drifts into the palace, and he's captivated. What is that sound, so lovely, so delightful?
It's a lute, your majesty, his servants say. Go, he says, bring me that sound. They bring him the lute.
He looks at it, a wooden body, some strings, and says: I don't want this. I want the sound. The servants are in for a long evening.
The Buddha tells this story near the end of the chapter on the senses.

teach.h: BODY, SKIN, ARM, STRINGS, A PLAYER
teach.b: In SN 35.246, the servants try to explain. This lute, your majesty, is made of many parts: a body, a skin, an arm, a frame, strings, a plectrum. And it sounds because a player puts in the right effort.
The king isn't satisfied. He splits the lute into ten pieces. Then a hundred.

teach.h: TEN PIECES, A HUNDRED, THEN ASHES
teach.b: Then he burns the pieces, and scatters the ashes in a strong wind, or lets the river carry them off. Then he says: a poor thing, this lute, whatever a lute is. People have been badly misled by it.
It's a funny scene. The king did exactly what a careful investigator does.

teach.h: THE SOUND IS IN NO ONE PART
teach.b: He took the thing apart, looking for where the sound lives, and it wasn't anywhere. Not in the strings, not in the wood, not in the ashes. The sound was real.
It came from the parts and the playing together, and couldn't be found in any one of them. Then the Buddha applies it.
In the same way, a monk investigates form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, as far as they go.

teach.h: I, MINE, I AM: NO LONGER THERE
teach.b: And when he does, whatever thoughts of I, or mine, or I am he used to have no longer come. Remember Vajira's chariot, a name for parts.
Here it's sound, something you can hear but not hold. The self, the sutta suggests, is looked for in the same way, and found in the same way.

how: In insight meditation, many Buddhists investigate body and mind part by part, much as the king searches the lute, to see that no single part is the self.

o: a flute played by a shepherd
a drum beaten in the palace

p: many parts and the player's effort
splits it, burns it, scatters it

s: the king finds the sound inside the strings
he splits the lute, burns it, scatters the ashes, and finds the sound nowhere.
the servants say the sound needs a player's effort
the lute sounds from its parts and the player together.
the sutta concludes that sound isn't real
the sound was real; it just couldn't be found in any one part.

games.q: you're the king. your servants bring you the lute whose sound you loved. you want the sound itself. what do you do?
o: ask a musician to play it again.
split it into pieces looking for the sound.
games.why: he splits it into ten, then a hundred pieces, burns them and scatters the ashes, and calls the lute a poor thing that misleads people.

practice: Look for yourself, gently, the way the king looked for the sound: is it in the feet, the hands, the breath, this passing thought, the feeling in the chest?

Go slowly, one part at a time, noticing that each part is there, that something is clearly happening, and that you can't find the one place where you live. No need to conclude anything; just keep looking, with curiosity.

wordCard.voice: Vina. The Pali and Sanskrit word for a lute, the instrument a king takes apart in SN 35.246 looking for its sound, applied to the search for a self. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit vina: a lute, the stringed instrument in SN 35.246, the Vinopama Sutta.

carryVoice: Your line: many parts, one sound. A king's long evening, and a lute in ashes. See you tomorrow.
